An alternative is to use shipboard type equipment to obtain the information. This would require drilling numerous holes through the ice in order to place sparkers and receivers. The cost of this exercise would be enormous and extremely time consuming, and has been rejected as a reasonable possibility.
Because the Ross Ice Shelf is moving seaward at a rate of about one meter per day at the tentative drill site, the maximum depth of sediment drilling becomes a function of the drilling rate versus depth of water. It seems unlikely that a penetration of more than 150-m will be possible.
Considerable discussion has been held concerning the matter of drilling "blind" into an unknown geologic environment. It is generally agreed that to drill to 100-m is safe, to 150-m is marginal, and anything deeper should be done very carefully and slowly.
Careful field examination of the core for traces of hydrocarbons will also be conducted and any significant increase in content will be taken as a sign of a hydrocarbon trap and the drilling operation halted.
In the very remote possibility that a trap, under sufficient pressure to be uncontrolled, is penetrated, there would be release of hydrocarbons onto the surface of the Ross Ice Shelf, and possibly beneath the ice shelf. There would be considerable impact on the surface of the Ross Ice Shelf and it is likely that the liquid hydrocarbon would spread out and percolate down to the firn-ice interface, filling the pore spaces. This pool of petroleum-soaked ice would eventually reach the front of the Ross Ice Shelf, be added to the marine environment and dispersed in the same manner as oil slicks elsewhere.
